subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is BIM?
subHeading: Understanding what BIM actually is, how it works and why it is much more than a 3D model.
abstract: BIM is a way of creating, managing and sharing information about a building or infrastructure project. Using a simple example, we explain how BIM connects people, models and information throughout a project's lifecycle.
body:
You may have heard people talking about **BIM**, but what does it actually mean?

BIM stands for **Building Information Modelling**.

At its simplest, BIM is a way of creating, managing and sharing information about a building or infrastructure project throughout its lifecycle.

And despite the name, **BIM is much more than a 3D model.**

## So, What Is BIM?

Imagine we're building a new apartment block.

An architect creates the architectural design. A structural engineer designs the foundations, columns, beams and slabs. Mechanical and electrical engineers design things like heating, ventilation, lighting and power.

A contractor then has to build everything on site.

Without a coordinated approach, each discipline can end up working with its own drawings, models and information.

BIM brings these different pieces of information together so that the project team can work from **coordinated and reliable information**.

The result is a digital representation of the asset that can contain both **geometry and information about the things being built**.

## It's More Than a 3D Model

A traditional 3D model might simply show us what a building looks like.

A BIM model can tell us much more.

For example, a wall might contain information about:

- Its dimensions and location
- What material it is made from
- Its fire rating
- Its construction type
- Its manufacturer
- Its relationship with other building elements

The model therefore becomes a place where information about the physical asset can be structured and managed.

Instead of simply seeing **a wall**, we can understand **what that wall actually is**.

## BIM Connects Different Disciplines

Let's go back to our apartment block.

The structural engineer has designed a beam.

The mechanical engineer has designed a ventilation duct.

If those two designs are developed independently, the duct could end up occupying the same space as the beam.

With coordinated BIM models, the teams can bring their information together and identify potential conflicts before construction reaches site.

The problem can then be resolved during design rather than discovered when someone is trying to physically build the system.

This is one of the major benefits of BIM:

> **Problems are often easier and cheaper to solve when they are found digitally before they become physical problems on site.**

## BIM Throughout the Project

BIM isn't only useful during design.

The information can develop as the project progresses.

During **design**, we might use BIM to understand the proposed building and coordinate different disciplines.

During **construction**, the information can support sequencing, quantities, fabrication and installation.

At **handover**, information about the completed asset can be provided to the owner or operator.

During **operation**, that information can help people understand, maintain and manage the building.

The model and information therefore have the potential to follow the asset throughout its lifecycle.

## What Makes BIM Different?

The important thing about BIM isn't simply that we have created a detailed digital model.

It's that the model is part of a wider **information management process**.

People need to know:

**What information do we need?**

**Who is responsible for producing it?**

**When is it needed?**

**Where is it stored?**

**Who needs to use it?**

These questions become increasingly important as projects become larger and more complicated.

## The Simple Definition

So, what is BIM?

You could think of it as:

> **A coordinated way of creating, managing and sharing information about an asset throughout its lifecycle.**

The 3D model is an important part of that process, but it is only one part.

BIM brings together **people, processes, information and technology** to help teams make better decisions about what they are designing, constructing and ultimately operating.

And that's the important distinction:

**BIM isn't about making a better-looking 3D model.**

**It's about managing information better.**

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: The Dimensions of BIM.
subHeading: Understanding how BIM moves from 3D geometry into time, cost, performance and the operation of an asset.
abstract: You may have heard of 3D, 4D, 5D and 6D BIM, but what do these dimensions actually mean? Using a residential apartment block as an example, we can see how additional layers of information build on the basic 3D model.
body:
You may often hear people talking about the dimensions of BIM — 3D, 4D, 5D and sometimes even 6D, 7D, 8D and beyond. But what exactly do these dimensions mean?

The terminology isn't completely standardised across the world. Different countries, companies and software providers can use the terms slightly differently. However, there are some conventions that apply broadly across the industry.

To understand the concept, let's take a simple example: **a residential apartment block**.

We can start with a three-dimensional model of the building and progressively add more information to it. Each additional "dimension" represents another way of using information about the asset.

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: LOD in BIM.
subHeading: A simple guide to understanding how a BIM element develops from an early concept into a detailed representation of the finished asset.
abstract: LOD describes how much graphical detail has been developed in a BIM model. Using a drainage pipe as an example, we follow the journey from a simple conceptual representation through to detailed construction and the installed asset.
body:
You may have come across the term **LOD** when talking about BIM. It stands for **Level of Detail**, and it is essentially a way of describing how much graphical detail has been developed in a model element.

Put simply:

> **LOD tells us how much detail we have modelled.**

But what does that actually mean?

Let's take a simple example — **a drainage pipe running through our residential apartment block**.

As the project develops, our understanding of the drainage system improves. The model therefore becomes progressively more developed.

**This is the basic idea behind LOD.**

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: LOIN in BIM.
subHeading: A simple guide to understanding what information a BIM model actually needs to contain, and why that information changes throughout a project's lifecycle.
abstract: LOIN defines the information actually needed from a BIM model for a particular purpose. Using a fire door as an example, we look at how the required geometry, data and documentation change from design through construction and into operation.
body:
You may have come across the term **LOIN** when talking about BIM. It stands for **Level of Information Need**.

Put simply:

> **LOIN tells us what information we actually need about something, and when we need it.**

The idea is simple: don't produce more information than you need, but don't leave out information that someone actually needs to do their job.

## What does LOIN actually mean?

LOIN is about defining the information required from a BIM model for a particular purpose at a particular point in a project.

That information can broadly be thought of in three areas:

- **Geometry** — what the object looks like, its size and location
- **Information** — data attached to the object
- **Documentation** — drawings, manuals, certificates and other supporting documents

Let's take a simple example — **a fire door in our residential apartment block**.

## One Door, Different Information Needs

At the early design stage, the architect might only need to know:

- Where the door is
- Its approximate size
- That it is a fire-rated door

That's enough to develop the design.

Later, the contractor needs more information.

They might need:

- Exact dimensions
- Fire rating
- Door type
- Manufacturer or product specification
- Installation requirements

After the building is completed, the facilities team may need something different again:

- Asset ID
- Manufacturer
- Model
- Serial number
- Warranty information
- Maintenance documentation

The **door hasn't changed**.

What has changed is **the information that people need from it**.

That's the basic idea behind LOIN.

## Why Do We Need LOIN?

BIM projects can contain an enormous amount of information.

The problem is that **more information isn't automatically better**.

If a model contains hundreds of properties that nobody needs, someone still has to create, check, maintain and update all of that information.

LOIN gives us a way to ask:

> **What information is actually needed for this purpose, at this point in the project?**

Instead of simply asking someone to "add more information", we can define exactly what is required.

This helps avoid both **too little information and unnecessary information**.

## LOIN vs LOD

This is where LOIN is often confused with LOD.

**LOD is mainly concerned with the graphical development of an element.**

For example:

> How accurately and completely have we modelled this fire door?

LOIN asks a broader question:

> **What information do we actually need about this fire door?**

That could include the geometry, but also the data and documents associated with it.

So you could think of it like this:

**LOD**

→ *How developed is the modelled object?*

**LOIN**

→ *What information about that object do we actually need?*

The two ideas work together, but they aren't the same thing.

## The Key Idea

LOIN is ultimately about **giving the right person the right information at the right time**.

For our fire door, that might mean:

**Design:**
*We need to know where it is and what type it is.*

**Construction:**
*We need to know exactly what we're installing.*

**Operation:**
*We need to know what asset we've got and how to maintain it.*

The goal isn't to fill the BIM model with as much information as possible.

**It's to provide the information that actually has a purpose.**

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: Who Are the Parties in BIM?
subHeading: A simple guide to understanding who asks for information, who coordinates it and who produces it on a BIM project.
abstract: BIM projects involve different organisations with different responsibilities for producing and managing information. Using a simple apartment building example, we explain the roles of the appointing party, lead appointed party and appointed party.
body:
You may have come across some slightly confusing terminology when reading about BIM:

**Appointing Party.**
**Lead Appointed Party.**
**Appointed Party.**

They sound complicated, but the basic idea is actually quite simple.

They're essentially different roles within the **chain of responsibility for producing and managing project information**.

Let's use a simple construction project to see how they fit together.

## The Basic Relationship

Imagine a client wants to build a new apartment block.

The client appoints a main contractor to design and construct the building.

The main contractor then appoints a number of specialist companies — perhaps a steelwork contractor, MEP contractor and façade contractor.

You can think of the relationship like this:

**CLIENT**

↓

**MAIN CONTRACTOR**

↓

**SUBCONTRACTORS / SPECIALISTS**

Each party has a different role in the information process.

## The Appointing Party

The **appointing party** is essentially the organisation receiving the information.

In our example, this is the **client**.

The client might say:

> "I need information about the building that allows me to understand what is being designed, constructed and eventually handed over to me."

The client therefore establishes what information is required and makes appointments with the organisations responsible for delivering it.

Think:

> **"I need this information."**

The appointing party is often the client, owner or employer, although it doesn't always have to be. The important thing is the role they are performing in that particular appointment.

## The Lead Appointed Party

The **lead appointed party** is the organisation directly appointed by the appointing party and responsible for coordinating information within its delivery team.

In our example, this could be the **main contractor**.

The client appoints the main contractor to deliver the project.

The main contractor then has to coordinate the information produced by the different teams working under its appointment.

For example:

- Structural contractor
- Steelwork contractor
- MEP contractor
- Façade contractor
- Specialist suppliers

The main contractor therefore isn't necessarily producing all the information itself.

It is responsible for **coordinating the information coming from the delivery team and providing the required information to the client**.

Think:

> **"I'm responsible for coordinating this information and getting it to the client."**

## The Appointed Party

The **appointed party** is the organisation providing information as part of the delivery team.

For example, our main contractor might appoint a specialist steelwork contractor.

The steelwork contractor could be responsible for producing information about:

- Steel members
- Connections
- Fabrication
- Installation
- Quantities
- Relevant specifications

They provide that information to the party that appointed them.

Think:

> **"I'm responsible for producing this information."**

## Putting It Together

Let's imagine our apartment building again.

The relationships could look something like this:

### Client

**Appointing Party**

> "I need the information required to deliver and operate my building."

↓

### Main Contractor

**Lead Appointed Party**

> "I'll coordinate the information from my delivery team and provide it to the client."

↓

### Steelwork Contractor

**Appointed Party**

> "I'll produce the information about the steelwork I'm responsible for."

↓

### Steel Fabricator

**Appointed Party**

> "I'll provide the information required for the fabrication of the steel."

The exact structure can become much more complicated on a large project, with multiple delivery teams and layers of appointments.

But the basic principle remains the same.

## One Important Detail

Here's where the terminology can initially become confusing.

**The same organisation can have different roles in different appointments.**

For example, imagine the main contractor has been appointed by the client.

In that relationship:

**Client → Main Contractor**

The client is the **appointing party** and the main contractor is the **lead appointed party**.

But the main contractor then appoints a steelwork contractor:

**Main Contractor → Steelwork Contractor**

Now the main contractor is the **appointing party for that appointment**, while the steelwork contractor is the **appointed party**.

So the terminology describes **the role being performed within a particular appointment**, rather than giving every company a permanent BIM title.

This is one of the most important things to understand.

## Why Does BIM Use These Terms?

The terminology helps make responsibility clearer.

Instead of simply saying:

> "The contractor needs to provide the model."

we can ask:

**Who is appointing them?**

**What information are they responsible for?**

**Who coordinates that information?**

**Who ultimately needs to receive it?**

This becomes particularly important on large projects where hundreds of organisations may contribute information to the overall project.

## The Simple Version

If you remember nothing else, remember this:

**Appointing Party**

→ **"I need the information."**

**Lead Appointed Party**

→ **"I'll coordinate the information and deliver it to you."**

**Appointed Party**

→ **"I'll produce the information I'm responsible for."**

The terminology might sound complicated, but the underlying idea is simply about **who asks for information, who coordinates it, and who produces it.**

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: BIM Acronyms.
subHeading: A simple guide to the key BIM information-management acronyms, and how they connect from organisational need through to asset operation.
abstract: BIM projects involve a chain of information requirements, plans, models and processes. Using a government highway agency delivering a new bridge as our example, we introduce OIR, AIR, PIR, EIR, BEP, PIM, AIM and CDE, and show how they fit together.
body:
If you have ever opened a BIM document and thought it looked like someone had thrown a handful of letters at you, you are not alone. OIR, AIR, PIR, EIR, BEP, PIM, AIM and CDE can make BIM information management sound much more complicated than it really is.

The underlying idea is actually quite simple: an organisation needs information, those needs are turned into requirements, the project team works out how to deliver them, information is produced and exchanged during the project, and the useful information is eventually handed over so the finished asset can be operated and maintained.

In this series, we are going to follow that process through one example: a government agency responsible for highways is planning a new bridge.

The Information Hierarchy

At the top level, the highway agency has a reason for needing information. It needs to understand its assets, manage its roads and bridges, plan maintenance and make decisions about future investment.

That organisational need starts a chain of requirements.

OIR — Organisational Information Requirements

The OIR describes the information the organisation needs to support its wider business objectives.

For our highway agency, that could mean information needed to manage its network, understand asset condition, plan maintenance or report on performance.

In simple terms:

“What information does the organisation need?”

AIR — Asset Information Requirements

The AIR takes that need and focuses it on the assets the organisation owns or manages.

For the new bridge, this could include information about its structure, components, materials, inspection requirements and maintenance needs.

The question becomes:

“What information will we need about the asset?”

PIR — Project Information Requirements

The PIR brings the focus onto the project itself.

The agency is now delivering a new bridge, so it needs information to make decisions, coordinate the design, construct the bridge and ultimately hand over the information needed to operate it.

In simple terms:

“What information do we need to deliver the project?”

EIR — Exchange Information Requirements

Information is not much use if nobody knows what needs to be exchanged, when it needs to be exchanged or what form it should take.

The EIR sets out the information that needs to be exchanged between the parties involved in the project.

For example, the highway agency may need certain design information from the design team and construction information from the contractor at defined stages.

The question becomes:

“What information needs to be exchanged?”

BEP — BIM Execution Plan

Now the project team needs to explain how it is actually going to make all of this happen.

The BIM Execution Plan sets out the approach for producing, managing, coordinating and exchanging information during the project.

It can cover things such as responsibilities, processes, software, information standards, naming conventions and delivery procedures.

In simple terms:

“How are we going to produce and manage the information?”

PIM — Project Information Model

As the project progresses, information is actually produced and developed.

The Project Information Model contains the information being developed and managed during the delivery of the bridge project.

That might include models, drawings, specifications, schedules and other project information.

This is where the requirements start becoming something tangible.

AIM — Asset Information Model

Eventually, the project reaches completion and the information needed to operate and maintain the bridge needs to be available for the asset owner.

The Asset Information Model contains the information needed to manage the completed asset throughout its operational life.

For our highway agency, this could include information about bridge components, inspection requirements, maintenance information and other useful asset data.

CDE — Common Data Environment

Running through all of this is the Common Data Environment.

The CDE is the controlled environment where project information is managed, shared and accessed according to the project's agreed processes.

It is important to think of the CDE as the environment supporting the information workflow rather than simply another step in the hierarchy.

Putting It All Together

The easiest way to remember the relationship is as a chain:

Need → Requirements → Plan → Produce → Exchange → Handover → Operate

The acronyms fit into that journey.

OIR establishes the organisation's information needs.

AIR considers the information needed about the assets.

PIR defines the information needed to deliver the project.

EIR defines what information needs to be exchanged.

The BEP explains how the project team will produce and manage that information.

The PIM develops as the project is delivered.

The relevant information is eventually handed over into the AIM so the completed bridge can be managed and maintained.

The CDE provides the controlled environment in which information is managed and shared throughout the process.

It is worth remembering that this is not simply a rigid document hierarchy where one document automatically becomes the next. The requirements flow from organisational need into asset and project needs, while the project team develops its processes and plans in response.

The Bigger Picture

The reason this hierarchy matters is simple: it helps prevent information from being produced just because somebody can produce it.

A bridge project can generate an enormous amount of information. Models, drawings, specifications, inspection records, schedules and data can quickly become overwhelming.

The goal of information management is not to create as much information as possible.

It is to make sure the right information gets to the right people at the right time, in a form they can actually use.

That is the idea we will follow throughout this series.

In the next articles, we will take each part of the hierarchy and look at it in more detail using our highway bridge as the case study.

The terminology might look complicated. The underlying idea isn't.

BIM information management is ultimately about answering one question: what information do people need, and how do we make sure they get it when they need it?

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: OIR - Organisational Information Requirements.
subHeading: Understanding what information an organisation needs to make decisions, manage its assets and deliver its wider business objectives.
abstract: OIR defines the information an organisation needs to make informed decisions and achieve its objectives. Using a government highway agency as our example, we explore how organisational goals around investment, risk, maintenance and performance create information needs, and how information from individual assets such as a bridge contributes to the bigger picture.
body:
If you are working through BIM terminology, OIR is one of those acronyms that can initially sound more complicated than it really is.

OIR stands for Organisational Information Requirements.

The important word is organisational.

OIR is not primarily about a particular building, bridge or project. It is about the information an organisation needs to run its business effectively and make informed decisions.

To understand it, let's continue with our example of a government agency responsible for a national highway network.

The agency is responsible for roads, bridges, tunnels, drainage, lighting and other infrastructure. It is also responsible for deciding where to spend money, managing risk, planning maintenance and reporting on the performance of the network.

So before we even think about the information needed to design our new bridge, we need to understand a much bigger question:

“What does the highway agency need to know to manage its organisation effectively?”

That is where OIR comes in.

OIR Starts With Organisational Goals

Imagine the highway agency's senior management team sitting down to plan the next five years.

They have thousands of assets to manage and a limited budget.

They need information to answer questions such as:

- Where should we invest our capital?
- Which parts of the network represent the greatest risk?
- Which assets are approaching the end of their useful life?
- How much will maintenance cost over the next decade?
- Are our infrastructure projects being delivered effectively?
- Are we meeting our safety and environmental objectives?
- Which parts of the network are performing well, and which need intervention?

These are organisational questions.

The agency needs information to answer them.

The OIR establishes those information needs.

Investment and Strategic Planning

One of the biggest responsibilities of a highway agency is deciding where its money should go.

It might need to understand the condition of its infrastructure, forecast future expenditure and identify where major investment will be required.

Our new bridge is only one small part of that picture.

Information about the bridge could eventually contribute to questions such as:

“How much investment is required across our bridge network over the next ten years?”

The organisation isn't interested in the bridge simply because it is a bridge.

It needs information about the bridge because that information contributes to a larger organisational decision.

Asset Risk and Condition

The agency also needs to understand the risks associated with its infrastructure.

It may need to know which asset types are deteriorating, where critical assets are located and where intervention may be required.

Again, our bridge becomes part of a much bigger question.

Information about its condition, inspections, age and maintenance history could contribute to the agency's understanding of the overall condition and risk of its bridge portfolio.

The OIR therefore isn't saying:

“We need the inspection history of Bridge 247.”

It is more like:

“What information do we need to understand and manage infrastructure risk?”

Maintenance and Operational Planning

Running a highway network involves constant maintenance.

The organisation needs to plan inspections, repairs, renewals and other interventions while keeping the network operating safely.

To do that effectively, it needs information about its assets.

Our bridge might eventually provide information about its components, maintenance requirements and inspection history.

But once again, the organisational question comes first:

“What information do we need to plan and manage our maintenance activities effectively?”

The bridge is one source of the information required to answer that question.

Performance and Reporting

Large organisations also need to measure how well they are performing.

The highway agency may have targets relating to network availability, safety, maintenance performance, project delivery, environmental performance, expenditure and asset condition.

This means the organisation needs reliable information that can be aggregated and analysed across its entire operation.

A single bridge might contribute a small amount of data to those wider measures.

The important distinction is that the organisation is interested in the performance of the network or portfolio, not simply the existence of one particular bridge.

Managing the Organisation's Information

There is another important organisational need: making sure information is actually usable.

If different projects record information in completely different ways, the agency may struggle to compare assets, analyse performance or make decisions.

The organisation therefore needs information that is consistent, accessible and suitable for the way it operates.

This is one of the reasons BIM information requirements matter.

The objective isn't to collect as much information as possible.

It is to collect the right information for the decisions the organisation needs to make.

So Where Does the Bridge Fit?

This is the important part.

Our bridge does not define the OIR.

The highway agency's organisational goals define the OIR.

The bridge is simply one asset through which those information needs eventually become relevant.

Think about the chain:

Organisational Goal

“We need to manage infrastructure risk.”

↓

Information Need

“We need reliable information about the condition and risk of our assets.”

↓

Asset

“Our new bridge is one of those assets.”

↓

Asset Information

“We therefore need appropriate information about that bridge.”

The same logic applies to investment, maintenance, performance and strategic planning.

The organisation starts with the question it needs to answer. The information requirements then flow down towards the assets and projects that can provide that information.

OIR vs Asset Information

This is where OIR is often confused with the Asset Information Requirements (AIR) that we will look at next.

A useful way to separate them is:

OIR asks:

“What information does our organisation need to make decisions and achieve its objectives?”

AIR asks:

“What information do we need about our assets to support those organisational needs?”

So if the highway agency wants to manage infrastructure risk, that is an organisational concern.

The information needed about individual bridges to assess that risk becomes an asset-level concern.

The two are connected, but they are not the same thing.

The Bigger Picture

OIR sits at the top of the information journey because it starts with the organisation itself.

It looks at the highway agency's objectives, responsibilities and decisions, rather than starting with a particular project or model.

From there, those needs can flow down into asset requirements, project requirements and eventually the information produced by project teams.

The simple way to remember it is:

“OIR is about what the organisation needs to know — not everything there is to know.”

Our bridge is important, but it is only one piece of a much larger information picture.

The organisation needs to understand its entire network, manage its risks, allocate its money, plan its maintenance and make decisions about the future.

The information from individual assets helps it do that.

That is the real purpose of OIR: connecting information to the decisions an organisation actually needs to make.

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: AIR - Asset Information Requirements.
subHeading: Understanding what information an organisation needs about its assets to operate, maintain and manage them effectively.
abstract: AIR defines the information an organisation needs about its assets to support operation, maintenance and management. Using our government highway agency and new bridge as the example, we explore the types of asset information that may be required and how AIR connects organisational goals to the information needed about individual assets.
body:
In the previous article, we looked at Organisational Information Requirements (OIR).

The highway agency in our example had some big questions:

Where should we invest? Which assets are becoming high risk? What maintenance will be required? How is the network performing?

Those are organisational questions.

But the agency cannot answer them using organisational information alone.

It needs information about the actual assets it owns and manages.

That is where Asset Information Requirements (AIR) come in.

From Organisational Need to Asset Information

Imagine our government highway agency is responsible for hundreds of bridges across its network.

The organisation wants to manage infrastructure risk effectively.

The OIR might therefore establish a need for information that allows the agency to understand the condition and risk of its infrastructure.

The next question is:

“What information do we need about our assets to support those organisational needs?”

That is the role of AIR.

The AIR translates higher-level organisational needs into information requirements relating to the assets themselves.

Our new bridge is one of those assets.

What Does the Agency Need to Know About the Bridge?

The answer is not simply “everything”.

A bridge can contain an enormous amount of information.

The agency could potentially collect thousands of pieces of data about its geometry, materials, components, inspections, documents and history.

But the purpose of AIR is to identify the information that is actually needed to manage the asset.

For our bridge, that might include several broad categories.

Asset Identity and Location

First, the agency needs to know what the asset is.

This could include:

- Bridge reference or asset ID
- Name
- Location
- Route
- Coordinates
- Asset type
- Construction date
- Ownership or responsibility

This sounds basic, but it becomes extremely important when an organisation manages hundreds or thousands of assets.

The agency needs to be able to identify the bridge, distinguish it from other bridges and connect its information to the wider asset register.

Physical and Technical Information

The agency also needs to understand what the bridge actually consists of.

For example:

- Structural form
- Materials
- Structural components
- Bearings
- Expansion joints
- Waterproofing
- Parapets
- Drainage components
- Other important systems

The important point is that AIR does not necessarily mean modelling every component in microscopic detail.

The question is:

“What information about the physical asset is needed to manage it?”

If a component is important to inspection, maintenance, safety or replacement, information about that component may become particularly valuable.

Condition and Inspection Information

For a highway agency, this can be one of the most important areas.

The organisation needs to understand whether its bridges are safe, serviceable and approaching the point where intervention is required.

Information could include:

- Inspection dates
- Inspection results
- Defects
- Condition ratings
- Structural issues
- Previous inspection records
- Recommended interventions
- Next inspection dates

Now we can see the direct connection back to the OIR.

The OIR said:

“We need to manage infrastructure risk.”

The AIR starts turning that requirement into something practical:

“We need condition and inspection information about our bridges so that we can understand and manage their risk.”

The organisational need has become an asset information need.

Maintenance Information

The agency also needs information that helps it look after the bridge throughout its operational life.

This could include:

- Maintenance activities
- Maintenance intervals
- Component replacement requirements
- Expected service lives
- Manufacturer information
- Access requirements
- Maintenance history
- Planned future works

For example, if a particular bridge component requires periodic inspection or eventual replacement, the agency needs information that allows it to plan for that work.

The bridge therefore becomes more than a completed construction project.

It becomes an asset with an ongoing maintenance requirement.

Operational and Safety Information

The bridge is also part of a live highway network.

The agency may therefore need information that helps it operate the asset safely.

This could include:

- Load restrictions
- Clearance information
- Traffic management requirements
- Operational constraints
- Emergency access information
- Safety-critical components
- Restrictions affecting the route

Again, the question is not:

“What information could we store?”

It is:

“What information will help us operate this asset safely and effectively?”

That distinction is important.

Lifecycle and Cost Information

The agency also needs to understand the financial implications of owning the bridge.

Information could include:

- Construction cost
- Major maintenance costs
- Component replacement costs
- Expected service lives
- Lifecycle cost information
- Planned future interventions

This information can then contribute to the wider organisational questions we explored in the OIR article.

For example, information from individual bridges can help the agency understand the future maintenance requirements of its entire bridge portfolio.

One bridge is therefore one piece of a much larger financial picture.

Supporting Documentation

Not all useful asset information is necessarily contained directly within a BIM model.

The agency may also need access to supporting documents such as:

- As-built drawings
- Structural calculations
- Inspection reports
- Maintenance records
- Manufacturer information
- Certificates
- Test results
- Warranties
- Photographs

These documents can form an important part of the information required to manage the completed asset.

The objective is not simply to have a highly detailed 3D model.

It is to have the information needed to understand and manage the asset.

AIR Is About the Asset — Not the Project

This distinction becomes particularly important as we move further down the information hierarchy.

Our highway agency has an organisational goal:

“Manage infrastructure risk effectively.”

That becomes an asset information need:

“Understand the condition and risk of each bridge.”

The bridge project then has to produce and deliver the information necessary to satisfy those requirements.

That is where Project Information Requirements (PIR) begin to enter the picture.

The PIR asks a different question:

“What information do we need to deliver this particular project?”

So the chain starts to look like this:

OIR

“What information does the organisation need?”

↓

AIR

“What information do we need about our assets?”

↓

PIR

“What information do we need to deliver the project?”

The three are connected, but each is asking a different question.

The Bigger Picture

AIR is where the information needs of the organisation start becoming much more tangible.

Instead of thinking about the highway agency as a whole, we can now look at the assets that make up its network.

For our bridge, that means understanding the information required to identify it, understand its construction and components, inspect it, maintain it, operate it safely and plan for its future.

But there is still an important principle to remember:

“AIR is not about collecting everything there is to know about an asset. It is about identifying what information is needed to manage it.”

The bridge is therefore not just a 3D model.

It is an asset with an identity, physical characteristics, condition, history, maintenance requirements, operational constraints and supporting information.

Once those asset-level information needs are understood, we can move another step down the hierarchy.

The next question becomes:

“How does the project actually produce and deliver the information we need?”

That is where Project Information Requirements (PIR) come in.

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: PIR - Project Information Requirements.
subHeading: Understanding what information is needed to successfully deliver a project, from early design through construction and handover.
abstract: PIR defines the information needed to successfully deliver a specific project. Using our government highway agency and new bridge as the example, we explore how project information supports design, coordination, programme, procurement, construction, quality and handover.
body:
So far in our BIM information hierarchy, we have worked from the top down.

The highway agency first established what information it needs to run its organisation. That gave us Organisational Information Requirements (OIR).

We then looked at what information the agency needs about the assets it owns and manages. That gave us Asset Information Requirements (AIR).

Now we have reached the project.

Our government highway agency has decided to build a new bridge.

The question is no longer:

“What information does the organisation need?”

or:

“What information do we need about our bridges?”

The question becomes:

“What information do we need to successfully deliver this particular project?”

That is where Project Information Requirements (PIR) come in.

From Asset Need to Project Need

The PIR takes the information needs associated with the project and considers what information will actually be required to plan, design, coordinate, construct and ultimately deliver it.

Our bridge project might involve:

- Civil engineers
- Structural engineers
- Geotechnical engineers
- Architects
- Surveyors
- Contractors
- Specialist suppliers
- Project managers
- The highway agency itself

All of these people will need information to do their jobs.

The PIR helps establish what that project needs to produce and manage.

It is therefore the point where the information requirements become much more closely connected to project delivery.

Design Information

The first obvious requirement is information needed to design the bridge.

The project team may need information about:

- Site conditions
- Existing infrastructure
- Topography
- Geotechnical conditions
- Structural requirements
- Highway geometry
- Drainage
- Utilities
- Environmental constraints
- Design standards and requirements

The important thing is that this information supports the design process.

For example, our structural engineer needs the relevant site and engineering information to develop the bridge structure.

The project doesn't simply need a model.

It needs the information required to make design decisions and produce a coordinated solution.

Coordination Information

A bridge project involves multiple disciplines working at the same time.

The structural engineer might be designing the bridge deck.

The highway engineer is working on the road alignment.

The drainage designer is developing the drainage system.

Utilities may need to be diverted.

Temporary works may need to be coordinated with the permanent works.

The project therefore needs information that allows these different disciplines to work together.

This could include:

- Models
- Drawings
- Spatial information
- Interface information
- Design reviews
- Clash or coordination information
- Design status

The objective is simple:

“Make sure the different parts of the project work together.”

Programme and Delivery Information

Information is also needed to understand when things need to happen.

The project may need:

- Programme information
- Design delivery dates
- Construction milestones
- Information delivery dates
- Approval dates
- Procurement dates
- Handover milestones

For example, the contractor cannot construct a bridge component if the required design information has not been produced, reviewed and approved.

Information therefore has a relationship with time.

The project needs to know not only what information is required, but when that information needs to be available.

Cost and Procurement Information

The project also needs information to support commercial decisions.

For example:

- Quantities
- Specifications
- Material requirements
- Cost information
- Work packages
- Procurement information
- Supplier information
- Construction requirements

Our bridge might require thousands of tonnes of materials, specialist components and multiple construction packages.

The project needs reliable information to allow those things to be estimated, procured and managed.

Again, the PIR is not necessarily saying exactly how every piece of information must be created.

It establishes the project’s information needs.

Construction Information

Once the design is developed, information needs to support the physical construction of the bridge.

This could include:

- Construction drawings
- Specifications
- Approved designs
- Method-related information
- Temporary works information
- Inspection requirements
- Testing requirements
- Quality records
- As-built information

The information is now supporting people working on the physical project.

A construction team needs to know what is being built, where it goes, what it needs to be made from and what requirements it needs to satisfy.

Quality, Compliance and Approvals

A major infrastructure project also needs information to demonstrate that the work has been properly designed, constructed and verified.

The project may therefore require information relating to:

- Design approvals
- Inspections
- Testing
- Material certification
- Quality records
- Non-conformances
- Regulatory requirements
- Safety requirements

This information can become particularly important later when the completed asset is handed over.

The project needs to be able to demonstrate not simply that the bridge was built, but that it was built in accordance with the required design, specifications and processes.

Handover Information

Although PIR is about delivering the project, the project does not exist in isolation.

Eventually, the completed bridge needs to become an operational asset.

That means the project needs to produce and collect information that supports the eventual handover.

For example:

- Final asset information
- As-built information
- Equipment and component records
- Maintenance information
- Inspection records
- Warranties
- Certificates
- Relevant drawings and models

This is where we can see the connection back to AIR.

The AIR established what information the organisation needs to manage the bridge.

The project therefore needs to make sure the required information is actually produced and captured during delivery.

PIR vs AIR

This distinction is worth making very clear because the two can sound almost identical.

AIR asks:

“What information do we need about the bridge so we can manage it as an asset?”

PIR asks:

“What information do we need to successfully deliver this bridge project?”

There is naturally some overlap.

For example, the highway agency may need information about the bridge’s bearings as part of its long-term maintenance strategy.

That's an AIR need.

The project may therefore need design information, specifications, installation records and testing information relating to those bearings.

Those are project information needs that help deliver the asset and eventually provide the information required for its operation.

The requirements are connected, but the questions are different.

Where Does PIR Sit in the Bigger Picture?

We can now extend our information journey.

OIR

“What information does the organisation need?”

↓

AIR

“What information do we need about our assets?”

↓

PIR

“What information do we need to deliver this project?”

↓

EIR

“What information needs to be exchanged?”

↓

BEP

“How are we going to produce and manage it?”

The PIR therefore sits at an important point in the hierarchy.

It takes the broader organisational and asset needs and brings them into the context of a specific project.

Our highway agency is no longer thinking about its entire bridge portfolio.

It is thinking about this bridge, this project, this delivery team and the information required to make the project successful.

The Bigger Picture

PIR is where information management starts becoming directly connected to project delivery.

The organisation has established what it needs.

The asset owner has established what it needs to know about its assets.

Now the project team needs to understand what information must be produced, managed and delivered to make the project happen.

And importantly, PIR is still about what information is needed, rather than exactly how every party will produce it.

That comes next.

The next question is:

“If all these people need to produce and exchange information, what exactly needs to be exchanged, when, between whom and in what form?”

That brings us to Exchange Information Requirements — EIR.

The simple way to remember PIR:

“OIR tells us what the organisation needs. AIR tells us what we need to know about the assets. PIR tells us what the project needs to deliver.”

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: EIR - Exchange Information Requirements.
subHeading: Understanding what information needs to be exchanged, who needs it, when it is needed and what it needs to contain.
abstract: EIR defines the information exchanges required to support a project. Using our government highway agency and new bridge as the example, we explore how information moves between designers, contractors and the client, and why the right information needs to reach the right people at the right time.
body:
By this point in our BIM information hierarchy, we have followed the information need from the organisation down to the project.

The highway agency established its organisational needs through Organisational Information Requirements (OIR).

It then identified the information it needs about its assets through Asset Information Requirements (AIR).

The specific bridge project then established what information it needs to successfully deliver the work through Project Information Requirements (PIR).

Now we reach the next question:

“If all of this information needs to be produced, how does it actually move between the people involved in the project?”

That is where Exchange Information Requirements (EIR) come in.

From Project Need to Information Exchange

Our highway agency is delivering a new bridge.

The project involves structural engineers, highway engineers, geotechnical specialists, contractors, surveyors, suppliers and the agency itself.

They all need to produce and receive information.

The structural engineer may need information from the geotechnical team.

The highway designer needs to coordinate with the structural designer.

The contractor needs approved design information.

The highway agency needs information from the delivery team so it can review progress and make decisions.

The problem is that simply saying “everyone needs information” isn't enough.

People need to know:

- What information needs to be exchanged?
- Who provides it?
- Who receives it?
- When does it need to be available?
- What does it need to contain?
- What format should it be provided in?
- What status should it have?
- What level of review or approval is required?

These are the questions EIR helps define.

EIR Is About the Exchange

Imagine our structural engineer has developed the preliminary bridge design.

The information is useful to the highway team, but the highway team cannot simply rely on whatever happens to be sitting on the structural engineer's computer.

There needs to be an agreed exchange.

For example:

“The structural team provides the coordinated structural design information to the highway design team at an agreed project stage, in an agreed format and with the required information for coordination and review.”

That is an information exchange.

The EIR establishes the requirements surrounding that exchange.

It is therefore useful to think of EIR as defining the information hand-offs that allow the project to function.

Who Needs to Exchange Information?

The first question is about the people and organisations involved.

Our bridge project might have:

- The highway agency
- Lead designer
- Structural engineer
- Highway engineer
- Geotechnical engineer
- Main contractor
- Specialist subcontractors
- Suppliers
- Surveyors

Each party has its own responsibilities.

The EIR helps establish what information needs to move between these parties.

For example, the structural team may need geotechnical information, while the contractor may need approved structural and highway information.

The exchange connects those responsibilities together.

What Information Needs to Be Exchanged?

The next question is what actually needs to move.

That could include:

- Models
- Drawings
- Specifications
- Schedules
- Reports
- Calculations
- Survey information
- Asset data
- Construction information
- Inspection records

The important point is that EIR is not saying that everything must be exchanged.

The project should identify the information exchanges that are actually necessary.

If information doesn't support a decision, activity, approval or deliverable, there may be little reason to exchange it.

When Does the Exchange Happen?

Information is only useful if it arrives when somebody needs it.

Imagine the contractor is preparing to construct the bridge deck.

The contractor needs the relevant design information before construction begins.

Likewise, a design team might need survey information before completing its design.

The EIR can therefore establish information exchanges around particular project stages or milestones.

For example:

Design development

↓

Coordination

↓

Review

↓

Approval

↓

Construction

↓

Handover

At each point, particular information may need to move between the project participants.

The timing matters.

What Does the Information Need to Contain?

Simply receiving a file does not necessarily mean the exchange has been successful.

The receiving party needs information that is suitable for its purpose.

For example, the highway agency may need a bridge model containing particular information for review.

The contractor may need approved drawings and specifications suitable for construction.

The asset team may need information about bridge components that will later support maintenance.

The EIR therefore helps establish the information content required for an exchange.

This connects directly back to the PIR.

The PIR asks:

“What information does the project need?”

The EIR takes that requirement and considers:

“What needs to be exchanged so that the project gets it?”

Format and Information Standards

Information also needs to be exchanged in a form that the receiving party can actually use.

Depending on the project, this could involve requirements around:

- File formats
- Naming
- Classification
- Metadata
- Model structure
- Document status
- Information containers
- Revision
- Approval

The exact requirements will depend on the project.

The important idea is that information exchange needs consistency.

If one organisation sends information in a completely different structure every time, the receiving team has to spend time interpreting and reorganising it.

Good information exchange makes the information easier to understand and use.

EIR Is Not Just About File Formats

This is an important distinction.

It would be easy to think of EIR as simply saying:

“Send us an IFC file every Friday.”

That's far too narrow.

An information exchange is about more than the file itself.

It involves:

Who

Who provides and receives the information?

What

What information is required?

When

When does it need to be exchanged?

Why

What activity, decision or requirement does it support?

How

What format, structure and process should be used?

The file is simply the container carrying the information.

The real question is whether the exchange delivers the right information to the right people at the right time.

EIR vs PIR

This is where the distinction between the two becomes particularly useful.

PIR asks:

“What information does the project need to successfully deliver the bridge?”

EIR asks:

“What information needs to be exchanged between the project participants to satisfy those needs?”

For example:

PIR

“The project needs coordinated structural and highway design information.”

↓

EIR

“The structural and highway teams need to exchange coordinated design information at the agreed project stage for review and coordination.”

The PIR defines the need.

The EIR defines the exchange required to satisfy that need.

Where Does EIR Sit in the Bigger Picture?

Our information journey now looks like this:

OIR

“What information does the organisation need?”

↓

AIR

“What information do we need about our assets?”

↓

PIR

“What information do we need to deliver the project?”

↓

EIR

“What information needs to be exchanged?”

↓

BEP

“How are we going to produce and manage it?”

This is an important point in the hierarchy because we are moving from requirements into delivery processes.

We know what the organisation needs.

We know what information is required about the bridge.

We know what the project needs to deliver.

Now we have identified the exchanges required to make that information available to the people who need it.

But there is still one big question.

Someone needs to work out exactly how the project team is going to make all of this happen.

Who produces each piece of information?

Which software will they use?

What standards will they follow?

How will models be coordinated?

How will information be reviewed and approved?

How will the Common Data Environment be used?

Those questions lead us to the next part of the hierarchy:

The BIM Execution Plan — BEP.

The Bigger Picture

EIR is essentially about the connections between information producers and information users.

A BIM project involves many organisations producing information for other organisations to use.

Without agreed exchanges, information can arrive too late, contain the wrong information, or be provided in a form that nobody can use effectively.

EIR helps define those information hand-offs.

The simple way to remember it is:

“PIR tells us what information the project needs. EIR tells us what information needs to move between people to provide it.”

The next question is then obvious:

“How are we actually going to organise all of this?”

That's where the BIM Execution Plan comes in.

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: BEP - BIM Execution Plan.
subHeading: Understanding how a project team will produce, manage and exchange the information required for a BIM project.
abstract: The BIM Execution Plan (BEP) explains how a project team will organise itself to produce, manage, coordinate and exchange information. Using our government highway agency and new bridge as the example, we explore how the BEP turns information requirements into practical processes for roles, responsibilities, coordination, standards, software, the CDE and information exchanges.
body:
The BIM Execution Plan, usually called the BEP, is the document that explains how a project team will actually manage BIM and information throughout a project.

So far in our information hierarchy, we have worked down from organisational needs to the requirements of a specific bridge project:

OIR → AIR → PIR → EIR

The EIR tells the project team what information needs to be exchanged.

The BEP then answers the practical question: “Okay — how are we actually going to do that?”

Using our government highway agency and its new bridge project, let's look at what the BEP is for, what it typically contains and how it connects the requirements to the work carried out by the project team.

## What is a BEP?

A BIM Execution Plan sets out the processes, responsibilities, methods and tools that the project team will use to produce and manage information.

It turns the project's information requirements into a practical way of working.

For example, the highway agency may require coordinated structural and highway information, information to be exchanged at defined project stages, models and drawings to follow agreed standards, information to be reviewed and approved, and asset information to be provided for handover.

Those requirements are useful, but they do not explain exactly how the project team will achieve them.

The BEP fills that gap.

It might define who is responsible for producing each type of information, which software and file formats will be used, how models will be structured, how information will be named and classified, how coordination and model reviews will work, how information will move through the CDE, when information will be exchanged, how issues will be identified and managed, and how the project team will deliver the required information at handover.

The BEP is therefore less about what information is wanted and more about how the team will organise itself to produce it.

## The Bridge Project Example

Imagine our highway agency has appointed a team to design and construct a new bridge.

The project involves a highway design team, structural engineers, geotechnical engineers, surveyors, environmental specialists, a main contractor, specialist subcontractors and the highway agency as client.

There are now a lot of people producing information.

Without an agreed way of working, problems can appear quickly.

The structural engineer might model the bridge using one naming convention while the highway team uses another. A survey might be issued in one coordinate system while a model uses another. The contractor might receive an outdated drawing. A model might be issued for information when it was actually expected to be approved.

The BEP exists to reduce this sort of confusion.

## What Does the BEP Define?

There is no single magic checklist that every project must use, but a BEP will generally explain how the team intends to manage the project's information.

### 1. Roles and Responsibilities

First, the team needs to know who is responsible for what.

For example:

Structural Team — responsible for the bridge structural model and associated structural information.

Highway Team — responsible for the road alignment, highway geometry and associated information.

Geotechnical Team — responsible for ground investigation and geotechnical information.

Contractor — responsible for construction information and information produced during delivery.

The BEP can define these responsibilities clearly so that information does not fall into the gap between different organisations.

### 2. Information Production

The BEP explains how information will actually be produced.

This can include modelling methods, drawing production, naming conventions, model structure, classification, coordinates and units, information containers, required software and file formats.

For example, the bridge team might agree that all discipline models will use the same project coordinate system.

That sounds like a small detail.

On a real project, it can be the difference between several models lining up correctly and several teams spending days trying to work out why they do not.

### 3. The Common Data Environment

The BEP also explains how the project team will use the CDE.

The CDE is where project information is managed and shared.

The BEP can define where information is stored, how information is named, who can access it, how revisions are controlled, how information moves through review and approval, and how superseded information is managed.

The important point is that the CDE is not simply a big folder in the cloud.

The project needs agreed rules for how information moves through it.

The BEP documents those rules.

### 4. Coordination and Review

A major purpose of BIM is allowing different disciplines to work with coordinated information.

The BEP can therefore define how coordination will happen.

For our bridge, the structural model might need to be coordinated with highway geometry, drainage, utilities, earthworks, geotechnical information, temporary works and construction requirements.

The BEP can establish when these models are combined, who performs the checks and how issues are recorded and resolved.

For example: The structural and highway teams exchange models at an agreed design stage. The coordination team reviews the combined information and records any issues requiring action.

Now everyone knows the process.

### 5. Information Exchanges

The EIR defines the required exchanges.

The BEP explains how the project team will make those exchanges happen.

For example:

EIR: The client requires coordinated bridge and highway design information at a defined project stage.

BEP: The structural and highway teams will produce their models using agreed standards, coordinate them through the CDE, perform defined reviews and issue the required information at the agreed milestone.

The requirement has become a working process.

That distinction is important.

### 6. Standards and Naming

Large projects can contain thousands of information containers.

If every organisation names its files differently, finding the correct information becomes difficult.

The BEP can therefore establish agreed conventions for file names, model names, drawing numbers, revisions, status codes, classifications, metadata and folder or container structures.

The aim is simple: people should be able to understand what information they are looking at without having to ask the person who created it.

### 7. Software and Technical Requirements

The BEP can also document the technical environment used by the project.

For example, the bridge project might use Civil 3D for highway design, Revit or another authoring platform for structural modelling, specialist software for geotechnical analysis, Navisworks for coordination and a CDE platform for information management.

The important thing is not necessarily which software is chosen.

The important thing is that the project team understands how the different tools fit together and how information moves between them.

## BEP vs EIR

This is one of the most useful distinctions to remember.

EIR: “What information needs to be exchanged?”

BEP: “How are we going to produce, manage and exchange it?”

For example:

EIR: The client requires coordinated bridge and highway design information at a defined project stage.

BEP: The structural and highway teams will produce their models using agreed standards, coordinate them through the CDE, perform defined reviews and issue the required information at the agreed milestone.

The EIR describes the requirement.

The BEP describes the response.

## How the BEP Fits Into the Information Hierarchy

We can now see the progression much more clearly.

OIR — What information does the organisation need?

AIR — What information does the organisation need about its assets?

PIR — What information is needed to successfully deliver this project?

EIR — What information needs to be exchanged, between whom and when?

BEP — How will the project team produce, manage and exchange that information?

The BEP is therefore where the project starts turning requirements into an agreed way of working.

## The BEP Is Not Just a Document

It is tempting to think of the BEP as another piece of paperwork that gets produced at the beginning of a project and then forgotten.

That misses the point.

The real value of the BEP is the process behind the document.

If the project changes, the way information is produced and managed may need to change too.

The BEP should therefore provide a reference point for the project team throughout delivery.

It helps answer practical questions such as:

Who produces this information?

Where should it be stored?

What format should it use?

When does it need to be issued?

Who reviews it?

What happens if there is an issue?

How does it eventually become part of the asset information?

## The Bigger Picture

Think back to our bridge project.

The highway agency started with organisational needs.

Those needs became asset information requirements.

The requirements for the bridge project became project information requirements.

Those requirements were translated into exchange requirements.

And now the BEP tells the project team how they are going to make all of this work in practice.

That gives us a simple chain:

Need → Requirements → Plan → Produce → Exchange → Handover → Operate

The BEP sits at the point where requirements become a plan for action.

## Key Takeaway

The EIR tells the team what information needs to be exchanged. The BEP explains how the team will organise itself to produce, manage, coordinate and exchange that information.

A good BEP gives everyone involved in the project a shared understanding of who does what, how they do it, when they do it and how the resulting information is managed.

And once the project starts producing that information, we arrive at the next part of the hierarchy: the Project Information Model — the PIM.

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: PIM - Project Information Model.
subHeading: Understanding what the Project Information Model contains, how it develops during delivery and how it supports the design and construction of an asset.
abstract: The Project Information Model (PIM) is the developing body of information created and managed during project delivery. Using our government highway agency and new bridge as the example, we explore how models, drawings, specifications, calculations, reports and construction information come together to form the PIM, how it relates to the BEP and EIR, and how relevant information eventually supports handover to the asset.
body:
So far in our BIM information hierarchy, we have looked at what information an organisation needs, what it needs to know about its assets, what is required to deliver a project, how information should be exchanged and how the project team will manage the process.

Now we reach the PIM — Project Information Model.

The PIM is the collection of information developed and managed by the project team during the delivery of a project.

Using our government highway agency and its new bridge as the example, we can see how the PIM develops from early design information into the information needed to construct and eventually hand over the completed asset.

## What Is a PIM?

PIM stands for Project Information Model.

At its simplest, the PIM is the project's developing body of information.

That can include much more than a 3D model.

For our bridge project, the PIM could contain structural models, highway models, drainage information, survey information, geotechnical information, drawings, specifications, calculations, schedules, reports, design information, construction information, inspection and testing records, approved information and as-built information.

The exact contents depend on the project and its information requirements.

The important point is that the PIM is the information being developed to deliver the project.

## Think of the PIM as the Project's Working Information

Imagine our highway agency has appointed a design team to develop a new bridge.

At the beginning of the project, there isn't a finished bridge model sitting somewhere waiting to be handed over.

Instead, information starts developing.

The survey team provides existing site information.

The geotechnical team provides information about the ground.

The highway team develops the road alignment.

The structural engineers develop the bridge.

Drainage designers develop the drainage system.

Other specialists contribute their own information.

All of this information develops as the project progresses.

That developing collection of project information forms the basis of the PIM.

## The PIM Changes as the Project Develops

One of the easiest ways to understand the PIM is to think about it as something that develops over time.

### Early Project

At the beginning, the information may be relatively limited.

The team might have existing surveys, site information, early design models, preliminary drawings, initial calculations, design assumptions and project requirements.

The bridge is still largely a design concept.

### Detailed Design

As the design develops, the PIM becomes richer.

The structural model becomes more defined.

The highway geometry develops.

Drainage is coordinated.

Interfaces between disciplines are reviewed.

Drawings and specifications are developed.

Calculations are produced.

Design decisions are recorded.

The project now contains much more information about what is going to be built.

### Construction

The information continues to develop during construction.

The project team may add construction drawings, approved technical information, inspection records, test results, material information, installation information, site records, changes and revisions, and construction progress information.

The PIM is therefore not simply the design model.

It can contain the wider project information required to support delivery.

## The PIM Is More Than a 3D Model

This is one of the most important points to understand.

A common misconception is: PIM = BIM model.

It isn't that simple.

A model is an important part of the PIM, but the PIM can contain many different types of information.

For our bridge, the project might contain a structural model showing the bridge geometry.

But the project may also need the structural calculations that justify the design.

It may need drawings showing reinforcement.

It may need specifications describing materials.

It may need inspection records showing that construction work has been checked.

It may need test results demonstrating that materials or components meet the required standards.

All of these contribute to the information required to deliver the project.

So rather than thinking PIM = one model, think PIM = the project's managed information as it develops through delivery.

## How Does the PIM Relate to the BEP?

The relationship between the BEP and PIM is particularly important.

The BEP describes how the team will manage information.

The PIM is the information that the team actually develops and manages.

For example:

BEP: The structural team will produce a coordinated structural model using agreed naming, classification, file formats and project coordinates.

PIM: The resulting structural model, together with the associated project information, becomes part of the information being developed for the bridge.

The BEP establishes the rules and processes.

The PIM is the resulting project information.

## How Does the PIM Relate to the EIR?

The EIR tells the project team what information needs to be exchanged.

The PIM is where that information is actually produced and managed during delivery.

For example, the EIR might require coordinated bridge and highway information at a particular project stage.

The project team then develops that information through its design and coordination processes.

The resulting models, drawings, reports and other information become part of the PIM.

So the relationship can be simplified as:

EIR → defines the required exchanges

BEP → defines how the team will deliver them

PIM → contains the information being developed

## What Happens to the PIM at Handover?

This is where the PIM becomes particularly important.

Eventually, the project reaches completion.

The highway agency now needs information about the finished bridge, not simply information about how the project was designed.

Some of the information developed during the project will therefore become useful for operating and maintaining the completed asset.

The project team needs to identify the information required for the next stage of the asset's life.

This leads us towards the AIM — Asset Information Model.

The relationship can be thought of simply as:

PIM → Information developed during project delivery

Handover → Relevant information is transferred and structured for the completed asset

AIM → Information needed to operate and manage the asset

The PIM does not simply disappear when construction finishes.

Relevant information from the project becomes part of the information needed to manage the asset.

## A Simple Bridge Example

Imagine the bridge has 24 bearings.

During the project, the PIM might contain bearing locations, bearing types, design information, manufacturer information, drawings, installation information, inspection records, test results, revisions and approval records.

Not all of this information will necessarily be needed throughout the bridge's entire operational life.

The project team therefore needs to determine which information is required for the completed asset.

For example, the highway agency may need to know:

Which bearings are installed?

Where are they located?

Who manufactured them?

When were they installed?

What maintenance or inspection requirements apply?

That operationally useful information can then form part of the asset information handed over for the bridge.

## PIM vs AIM

This distinction is worth remembering.

PIM — Project Information Model: Information developed and managed during the delivery of the project.

AIM — Asset Information Model: Information needed to operate, maintain and manage the completed asset.

A useful way of thinking about it is:

The PIM helps you deliver the asset. The AIM helps you manage the asset.

There can obviously be overlap between the two.

The important distinction is the purpose of the information.

## Where Does the CDE Fit?

The PIM also connects directly to the Common Data Environment, or CDE.

The CDE is the managed environment through which project information is stored, shared, reviewed and controlled.

The PIM is the information.

The CDE is the environment used to manage that information.

So:

PIM ≠ CDE

The PIM is what the project produces.

The CDE is where and how that information is managed and shared.

This distinction becomes much easier when you stop thinking of BIM as just a collection of software tools.

The model, documents, processes, people and information all have different roles.

## The Bigger Picture

Let's return to our information hierarchy.

The government highway agency starts with a business need.

OIR — What information does the organisation need?

AIR — What information does it need about its assets?

PIR — What information is needed to deliver this bridge project?

EIR — What information needs to be exchanged?

BEP — How will the team produce and manage it?

PIM — What information is actually being developed during the project?

AIM — What information is needed to operate the completed bridge?

The PIM is therefore the point where the information requirements and agreed processes become the actual information being developed by the project team.

## Key Takeaway

The Project Information Model is the developing body of information created and managed during project delivery.

It is not simply a 3D model.

It can include models, drawings, specifications, calculations, reports, schedules, surveys, construction information, inspection records and other information required to deliver the project.

The BEP explains how the information will be produced and managed.

The PIM is the information being produced and managed.

And when the project reaches completion, relevant information from the PIM can move into the information needed to operate the finished asset — the AIM.

The PIM helps you deliver the asset. The AIM helps you manage the asset.

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: AIM - Asset Information Model.
subHeading: Understanding what information is needed to operate, maintain and manage an asset throughout its life.
abstract: The Asset Information Model (AIM) is the collection of information needed to operate, maintain and manage a completed asset.
