Using our government highway agency and new bridge as the example, we explore how project information transitions from the PIM into an operational asset information model and how the AIM supports inspections, maintenance, safety, asset management and lifecycle decisions.
body:
Our bridge project has now reached an important point.

The design has been completed. Construction is finished. The bridge is open to traffic.

But the highway agency's job does not end when the contractor leaves site.

For the next 30, 50 or even 100 years, the agency needs to operate, inspect, maintain and manage that bridge.

To do that effectively, it needs information.

This is where the AIM — Asset Information Model — comes in.

## What Is an AIM?

AIM stands for Asset Information Model.

The AIM is the collection of information needed to operate, maintain and manage a completed asset.

For our government highway agency, that means information about the finished bridge that can support its ongoing lifecycle.

The AIM might contain information about the bridge's identity and location, structural components, materials, bearings, expansion joints, parapets, drainage, inspections, defects, maintenance, replacements, warranties, manufacturer information, safety requirements, asset condition and supporting documents, photographs and drawings.

The exact information required depends on what the asset owner needs to manage the asset.

The important point is that the AIM is focused on the asset's operational life.

## From Project to Asset

This is where the distinction between the PIM and AIM becomes particularly useful.

During the project, the team is focused on: “What information do we need to design and construct this bridge?”

That information forms part of the PIM.

Once the bridge is complete, the highway agency is asking a different question: “What information do we need to operate and maintain this bridge?”

That information forms the basis of the AIM.

The transition can be thought of as:

PIM → Information developed during project delivery

Handover → Relevant information is identified, verified and transferred

AIM → Information required to manage the completed asset

The PIM helps deliver the bridge.

The AIM helps manage the bridge.

## What Information Does the AIM Contain?

Let's return to our bridge.

The highway agency may have thousands of pieces of information relating to it.

But not all project information is equally useful once construction is finished.

The AIM focuses on the information that has value during the asset's operational life.

### 1. Asset Identity

First, the agency needs to know what asset it is dealing with.

For example: Bridge ID, bridge name, route, location, coordinates, asset type, ownership, responsible organisation, construction date and opening date.

This information allows the agency to identify the bridge within its wider asset portfolio.

### 2. Physical and Technical Information

The agency needs to understand what the bridge actually consists of.

The AIM might contain information about bridge type, span arrangement, structural system, materials, deck, piers, abutments, bearings, expansion joints, parapets, drainage components, waterproofing and other important components.

This information gives the asset owner a digital record of the physical asset.

### 3. Inspection and Condition Information

Bridges need to be inspected throughout their lives.

The AIM can therefore connect the bridge to its inspection history.

For example:

2027 — routine inspection completed.

2030 — defect identified at expansion joint.

2031 — repair completed.

2034 — next inspection due.

Over time, this creates a history of the asset's condition and interventions.

The agency can use that information to make better maintenance decisions.

### 4. Maintenance Information

The AIM can also contain information needed to plan and carry out maintenance.

For example, the bridge's expansion joints may have an expected service life.

The agency might need to know when they were installed, who manufactured them, what type they are, inspection requirements, maintenance requirements, expected replacement period, previous maintenance and replacement records.

Instead of starting from scratch every time maintenance is required, the agency has a structured record of the asset.

### 5. Operational and Safety Information

Some information exists specifically to help the agency operate the asset safely.

For our bridge, this might include load restrictions, vehicle height restrictions, clearances, traffic restrictions, emergency access information, safety-critical components, inspection requirements and operational constraints.

This information can become particularly important during incidents or unusual events.

### 6. Supporting Documents

The AIM does not have to contain every document ever produced during the project.

Instead, it should contain or provide access to the documents needed to support asset management.

For example: as-built drawings, inspection reports, maintenance records, manufacturer manuals, certificates, warranties, test records, photographs and asset registers.

The important question is not: “Can we hand over everything?”

It is: “What information will the asset owner actually need?”

That distinction prevents the AIM from becoming a digital dumping ground.

## The AIM Should Be Useful, Not Just Complete

This is one of the most important ideas behind asset information management.

Imagine the contractor hands the highway agency 50,000 files at the end of the project.

Technically, the agency has received a huge amount of information.

But suppose nobody can easily answer:

Which bearings are installed?

Where are they?

When were they installed?

When do they need inspection?

What manufacturer supplied them?

The agency has received information, but it has not necessarily received useful asset information.

The AIM should therefore be structured around the decisions and activities the asset owner needs to perform.

Information should have a purpose.

## AIM and Asset Management

The AIM becomes particularly valuable when it is connected to the organisation's wider asset-management processes.

Imagine the highway agency manages 800 bridges, 2,000 culverts, 15,000 drainage assets and hundreds of kilometres of road.

The agency does not just need information about one bridge.

It needs to manage an entire portfolio.

The AIM allows information about the individual bridge to contribute to that wider picture.

For example, the agency could identify bridges approaching major maintenance, components reaching the end of their service life, assets with recurring defects, assets requiring inspection, assets with elevated risk and maintenance expenditure across the portfolio.

This connects the individual asset back to the organisation's wider information needs.

And that takes us right back to the beginning of our hierarchy.

## OIR → AIR → AIM

Remember the OIR?

The highway agency might have an organisational objective to manage its bridge network safely and efficiently.

That creates information needs.

The AIR then defines what information the organisation needs about its assets to support those objectives.

The project develops and hands over that information.

The AIM contains the information required to manage the completed bridge.

So the relationship can be viewed as:

OIR → What information does the organisation need?

AIR → What information does it need about its assets?

PIM → What information is developed during the project?

Handover → Relevant information is transferred

AIM → What information is needed to operate and manage the completed asset?

The hierarchy has now come full circle.

## AIM vs PIM

This distinction is worth making very clear.

PIM — Project Information Model: Purpose: Deliver the project. Contains information developed during design and construction. Examples include design models, drawings, calculations, specifications, construction information, inspection and testing information and project records.

AIM — Asset Information Model: Purpose: Manage the completed asset. Contains information needed for operation, maintenance and asset management. Examples include asset identity, component information, inspection history, maintenance requirements, condition information, warranties, operational constraints and as-built information.

There will naturally be overlap.

The key difference is why the information is being used.

PIM = information for delivering the asset.

AIM = information for managing the asset.

## Where Does the CDE Fit?

The CDE still plays an important role.

The CDE is the controlled environment used to manage and share information.

The PIM and AIM are collections of information.

The CDE provides the environment and processes through which that information can be managed.

During the project, the CDE supports the development and management of the PIM.

At handover, relevant information can be transferred and structured for the asset owner's operational needs.

That information then supports the AIM.

So again:

PIM/AIM = the information

CDE = the managed environment

## The Bridge After Handover

Let's imagine our bridge ten years after completion.

A maintenance engineer receives a report that one of the bridge's expansion joints is showing signs of deterioration.

Instead of searching through old project folders, they can access the asset's information.

They can identify the component, see where it is located, find its manufacturer and installation information, review previous inspections, check maintenance history and look at relevant drawings and documents.

The information supports a real decision about a real asset.

That is the point of the AIM.

The information has become useful because it is connected to the asset and the decisions people need to make about it.

## The Bigger Picture

We can now see the full journey:

OIR — What information does the organisation need?

AIR — What information does it need about its assets?

PIR — What information is needed to deliver the project?

EIR — What information needs to be exchanged?

BEP — How will the team produce and manage it?

PIM — What information is developed during the project?

Handover

AIM — What information is needed to operate and manage the completed asset?

The information journey does not end when construction finishes.

In many ways, that is when the information starts doing its most important job.

## Key Takeaway

The Asset Information Model is the information needed to operate, maintain and manage an asset throughout its lifecycle.

For our bridge, that means giving the highway agency reliable information about the asset, its components, condition, inspections, maintenance, safety requirements and supporting documentation.

The PIM helps the project team deliver the bridge.

The AIM helps the asset owner manage the bridge.

And that is the real purpose of the information hierarchy: create the right information during delivery so that it remains useful throughout the life of the asset.
